cards.front: What is an ACTIO IN REM, and who has capacity to sue and to be sued?
cards.back:
An ACTIO IN REM (property claim) enforces a right in rem; ACTIONES IN PERSONAM enforce relative claims.
• Claimant: the person asserting the property right.
• Defendant: the person possessing the thing and denying that right.
• Ex 27: a claim against a non-possessor fails.

cards.front: What are the two stages of the Roman formulary procedure?
cards.back:
Proceedings IN IURE before the PRAETOR, then proceedings APUD IUDICEM before the IUDEX.
• PRAETOR: elected magistrate; his edict lists the ACTIONES and EXCEPTIONES he grants.
• He grants an edictal ACTIO, creates ACTIO IN FACTUM / UTILIS, or denies (DENEGATIO ACTIONIS).
• IUDEX: private citizen who establishes the facts, then condemns or acquits.

cards.front: What is the LITIS CONTESTATIO, and why is the formula a 'hypothetical judgement'?
cards.back:
LITIS CONTESTATIO ends IN IURE: the praetor appoints the IUDEX and issues the formula.
• The formula contains the ACTIO and any EXCEPTIONES.
• 'If the claim is shown true, condemn; if not, acquit.'
• The praetor does not verify the facts; the IUDEX does.

cards.front: Which three actions protect ownership?
cards.back:
REI VINDICATIO, ACTIO PUBLICIANA and ACTIO NEGATORIA.
• REI VINDICATIO: civil-law owner who lost possession, against the possessor.
• ACTIO PUBLICIANA: the same aim for the usucapient.
• ACTIO NEGATORIA: against all other third-party interference.

cards.front: What are the three parts of the REI VINDICATIO formula?
cards.back:
INTENTIO (foundation of the claim), CLAUSULA ARBITRARIA (unless restored), CONDEMNATIO (pay the value, or acquit).
• INTENTIO: SI PARET REM … EX IURE QUIRITIUM AULI AGERII ESSE.
• CLAUSULA ARBITRARIA: NEQUE EA RES RESTITUETUR — IUSSUM DE RESTITUENDO pressures return.
• CONDEMNATIO: QUANTI EA RES ERIT; malicious refusal → claimant's IUSIURANDUM IN LITEM.

cards.front: Who may bring a REI VINDICATIO, and what must he prove?
cards.back:
Only the quirite owner (DOMINIUM EX IURE QUIRITIUM); he bears the burden of proving it.
• Bonitarian owner cannot (Ex 29 Alcesimus) — he uses the ACTIO PUBLICIANA.
• Chain of owners back to an original acquisition: PROBATIO DIABOLICA.
• Not proven → the IUDEX acquits (ABSOLVITO).

cards.front: What does OMNIS CONDEMNATIO PECUNIARIA EST mean for the REI VINDICATIO?
cards.back:
Every condemnation is for money: the IUDEX cannot order return of the thing itself.
• The defendant pays its estimated value at judgment (QUANTI EA RES ERIT).
• Return is only induced through the CLAUSULA ARBITRARIA.

cards.front: What is an EXCEPTIO, where does it stand in the formula, and who bears the burden of proof?
cards.back:
A defence: the ACTIO's wording favours the claimant, but outside considerations favour the defendant.
• Inserted right after the INTENTIO.
• INTENTIO (positive foundation): plaintiff proves; EXCEPTIO (negative foundation): defendant proves.
• Ex 28 (D 39.5.25): EXCEPTIO DOLI against the donor's REI VINDICATIO.

cards.front: EXCEPTIO DOLI PRAETERITI (SPECIALIS) vs PRAESENTIS (GENERALIS) — what is the difference?
cards.back:
PRAETERITI: plaintiff acted fraudulently in the past; PRAESENTIS: bringing the claim itself is a breach of faith.
• SI IN EA RE NIHIL DOLO MALO AULI AGERII FACTUM SIT NEQUE FIAT.
• Ex 30: Tullius knowingly took MANCIPATIO without CAUSA → PRAETERITI; realised later → PRAESENTIS.

cards.front: Against whom does the REI VINDICATIO lie (UBI REM MEAM INVENIO, IBI VINDICO)?
cards.back:
Against any possessor: 'wherever I find my thing, there I vindicate it'.
• The quirite owner's claim against a non-owner in possession.
• Presupposes the thing still exists; destruction ends ownership.
• Ownership is also lost when another acquires original ownership.

cards.front: Which remedies can prepare a REI VINDICATIO?
cards.back:
Interdicts settle who possesses; ACTIO AD EXHIBENDUM and INTERDICTUM QUEM FUNDUM push the possessor to defend.
• UTI POSSIDETIS (land), UTRUBI (movables): the defendant's role is better (Ex 31).
• No duty to defend IN REM; AD EXHIBENDUM (IN PERSONAM): produce the thing in court.
• Refusal to defend → plaintiff may seize it.

cards.front: Which possessors can be sued, and who are FICTI POSSESSORES (PRO POSSESSIONE DOLUS EST)?
cards.back:
Possessors; and non-possessors treated as possessors because 'fraud replaces possession'.
• Fraudulently defending without possessing, or giving up possession after LITIS CONTESTATIO.
• D 6.1.9: Pegasus demanded interdictive possession.
• Ulpian: any natural possessor able to restore (FACULTAS RESTITUENDI).

cards.front: What is the principle of RESTITUERE, and which fruits must the defendant restore?
cards.back:
The plaintiff is placed as if the thing had been returned at LITIS CONTESTATIO.
• Fruits since LC: FRUCTUS PERCEPTI and PERCIPIENDI (NEGLECTI); Ex 32: 150, not 100.
• Good or bad faith is irrelevant after LC.
• Before LC: BONAE FIDEI POSSESSOR owns separated fruits; MALAE FIDEI commits FURTUM.

cards.front: The thing perishes between LITIS CONTESTATIO and judgment — is the defendant liable?
cards.back:
Sources diverge: three liability models that cannot be reconciled.
• Possession-based: no longer possessor → not liable, unless DOLUS (fiction of possession).
• RESTITUERE (Proculians): always liable — DOLUS, CULPA, even CASUS.
• Sabinians: liable for any fault — DOLUS or CULPA.

cards.front: Paulus D 6.1.16.1: after LITIS CONTESTATIO, B sends the vindicated ship to sea in the sailing season; it sinks. Is B liable?
cards.back:
No — sailing in the proper season is not negligent; Paulus holds liable only for CULPA (and DOLUS).
• Liable if he entrusted the ship to unsuitable persons: CULPA IN ELIGENDO.
• He need not idle the ship — he owes FRUCTUS PERCIPIENDI anyway.

cards.front: What can a BONAE FIDEI POSSESSOR claim for his expenses against the vindicating owner?
cards.back:
Refund of value-increasing expenses (IMPENSAE), enforced by retaining the thing (RETENTIO) until paid.
• Procedurally: EXCEPTIO DOLI (PRAESENTIS) — the unpaid owner's claim counts as malicious.
• D 6.1.37: building after learning the truth → no EXCEPTIO, only IUS TOLLENDI.

cards.topic: 03.11. Protection — ACTIO PUBLICIANA and ACTIO NEGATORIA
cards.front: On what fiction is the ACTIO PUBLICIANA based, and how does its formula differ?
cards.back:
The plaintiff is treated as quirite owner as if the usucaption period (1 year movables, 2 land) had elapsed.
• Only the INTENTIO differs from the REI VINDICATIO.
• Requires TRADITIO on a IUSTA CAUSA (model formula: purchase).

cards.topic: 03.11. Protection — ACTIO PUBLICIANA and ACTIO NEGATORIA
cards.front: Who can bring the ACTIO PUBLICIANA, and what must he prove?
cards.back:
Anyone fulfilling all usucaption requirements except the elapse of time.
• Usucapients acquiring from a non-owner or on a putative title.
• Bonitarian owners (RES MANCIPI by TRADITIO).
• Civil-law owners — avoids PROBATIO DIABOLICA; proof of TRADITIO on valid title suffices.

cards.topic: 03.11. Protection — ACTIO PUBLICIANA and ACTIO NEGATORIA
cards.front: What is the EXCEPTIO IUSTI DOMINII?
cards.back:
The quirite owner's defence against a usucapient's ACTIO PUBLICIANA: SI EA RES NUMERII NEGIDII NON SIT.
• If he proves his ownership, the claim fails.
• So the usucapient stays weaker than the present owner.

cards.topic: 03.11. Protection — ACTIO PUBLICIANA and ACTIO NEGATORIA
cards.front: How does the bonitarian owner prevail against the vendor who is still quirite owner?
cards.back:
By EXCEPTIO or REPLICATIO REI VENDITAE ET TRADITAE; the vendor keeps only NUDUM IUS QUIRITIUM.
• Vendor's REI VINDICATIO → EXCEPTIO REI VENDITAE ET TRADITAE (or EXCEPTIO DOLI).
• Buyer's PUBLICIANA, vendor pleads IUSTI DOMINII → REPLICATIO REI VENDITAE ET TRADITAE.
• Other IUSTA CAUSA than sale → EXCEPTIO / REPLICATIO DOLI.

cards.topic: 03.11. Protection — ACTIO PUBLICIANA and ACTIO NEGATORIA
cards.front: Pomponius (Iulianus) D 21.3.2: T buys S's land from Titius; Titius inherits from S, then sells and delivers it to M. Can T reclaim it?
cards.back:
Yes — T's ACTIO PUBLICIANA against M succeeds.
• Titius' later inheritance cures the defect: T becomes bonitarian owner (convalescence).
• Titius keeps only NUDUM IUS QUIRITIUM: NEMO PLUS IURIS TRANSFERRE POTEST QUAM IPSE HABET.

cards.topic: 03.11. Protection — ACTIO PUBLICIANA and ACTIO NEGATORIA
cards.front: Unauthorised vendors sell the same thing to two buyers — who is stronger (Neratius vs Julian/Ulpian)?
cards.back:
Neratius: the buyer who first received delivery; Julian/Ulpian (different vendors): whoever is in possession.
• Neratius D 19.1.31.2: analogy to the owner's double sale — first TRADITIO wins.
• Ulpianus (Iulianus) D 6.2.9.4: the antithetical view.

cards.topic: 03.11. Protection — ACTIO PUBLICIANA and ACTIO NEGATORIA
cards.front: What is the ACTIO NEGATORIA for?
cards.back:
The owner's action declaring that an alleged servitude or other right to interfere does not exist.
• Also demands restoration of the prior state.
• Also wards off immissions (cheese-dairy smell, steam, stone chips).
• No right claimed → INTERDICTUM QUOD VI AUT CLAM against forcible or secret changes.

cards.topic: 03.11. Protection — ACTIO PUBLICIANA and ACTIO NEGATORIA
cards.front: Exegesis: a Digest fragment is about REI VINDICATIO — which questions should your interpretation address?
cards.back:
Who claims what from whom, on which basis — then defences and restitution.
• Plaintiff quirite owner (else ACTIO PUBLICIANA)? Defendant possessor (or FICTI POSSESSORES)?
• EXCEPTIONES (DOLI, REI VENDITAE ET TRADITAE, IUSTI DOMINII) and REPLICATIONES?
• Restitution: fruits, liability for destruction, expenses and RETENTIO of the BONAE FIDEI POSSESSOR.

cards.front: What are servitudes, and which types does Roman law distinguish?
cards.back:
Limited rights in rem in another's property: the owner must tolerate an act or refrain from one.
• Praedial (rural or urban) vs personal servitudes.
• NULLI RES SUA SERVIT (Paulus D 8.2.26): no servitude in one's own property.
• Holder acquires the burdened property → servitude ends (CONFUSIO).

cards.front: What does SERVITUS IN FACIENDO CONSISTERE NEQUIT mean?
cards.back:
A servitude cannot oblige the owner to act — only to permit or to refrain.
• Exception: IUS ONERIS FERENDI — the servient owner must keep the supporting building in repair.

cards.front: What is a praedial servitude?
cards.back:
A right of the current owner of land in another's land, facilitating use of his own.
• PRAEDIUM DOMINANS (benefitted) vs PRAEDIUM SERVIENS (burdened).
• Tied to the land; passes with it on sale (Ex 33).
• Modern term: easement.

cards.front: Name the rural praedial servitudes.
cards.back:
Servitudes of passage, water and pasture.
• Passage: ITER (on foot/riding), ACTUS (driving cattle), VIA (driving a vehicle).
• Water: AQUAE DUCTUS (conducting water), AQUAE HAUSTUS (drawing water).
• Pasture: IUS PASCENDI.

cards.front: Name the urban praedial servitudes.
cards.back:
Servitudes of building, support and drainage.
• Building: IUS ALTIUS NON TOLLENDI (no higher building), IUS LUMINIS (light, view).
• Support: IUS TIGNI IMMITTENDI (insert a beam), IUS ONERIS FERENDI (rest one's building).
• Drainage: IUS STILLICIDII (dripping), IUS FLUMINIS (diverting rainwater), IUS CLOACAE (sewage).

cards.front: Which principles limit servitudes (VICINITAS, UTILITAS, CIVILITER EXERCENDA)?
cards.back:
The estates must adjoin and the servitude must benefit the dominant estate; exercise it considerately.
• No mere personal pleasure, eg walks or meals (Paulus D 8.1.8 pr).
• SERVITUS CIVILITER EXERCENDA EST: least inconvenience to the servient owner.
• No unilateral extension: 20 sheep cannot become 40 (Ex 34).

cards.front: How does Paulus define USUSFRUCTUS (D 7.1.1)?
cards.back:
USUSFRUCTUS EST IUS ALIENIS REBUS UTENDI FRUENDI SALVA RERUM SUBSTANTIA.
• Right to use (USUS) and take fruits (FRUCTUS) of another's thing, preserving its substance.
• Most extensive personal servitude; ends with the holder's death.
• Ex 35: Hera may live in or rent the house, not convert it.

cards.front: Usufruct: which fruits belong to the usufructuary, and what must he promise the owner?
cards.back:
The recurrent proceeds, including rent (FRUCTUS CIVILES); the substance stays untouched.
• PARTUS ANCILLAE is no fruit → owner; the young of animals → usufructuary.
• Herd (UNIVERSITAS RERUM): replace dead animals with young ones.
• CAUTIO USUFRUCTUARIA: promise to use BONI VIRI ARBITRATU.

cards.front: Which personal servitudes exist besides usufruct, and how does usufruct differ from loan or lease?
cards.back:
USUS, HABITATIO, and OPERAE SERVORUM or ANIMALIUM.
• USUS: right to use only, without fruits.
• Loan, lease, usufructuary lease: contracts enforced IN PERSONAM, not rights in rem.

cards.front: How is the holder of a servitude protected (VINDICATIO SERVITUTIS vs ACTIO NEGATORIA)?
cards.back:
By interdicts modelled on the possessor's and by VINDICATIO SERVITUTIS (ACTIO CONFESSORIA), an action in rem.
• CONFESSORIA: declares the servitude exists and demands conforming conduct.
• NEGATORIA (owner's counterpart): declares it does not exist.
• Usufructuary of land: INTERDICTUM UTI POSSIDETIS UTILE.

cards.front: What is USUCAPIO LIBERTATIS?
cards.back:
The owner usucapts freedom from a servitude the holder does not exercise (NON USUS).
• Period: one year for movables, two years for land.
• Over buildings: owner must also create a contrary state, eg build higher.
• Distinct from usucaption of a servitude (barred for praedial ones: LEX SCRIBONIA).

cards.front: What are 'legal servitudes'?
cards.back:
Restrictions in favour of neighbours arising directly from statute, not from agreement.
• Neighbour may collect fallen fruit every other day: INTERDICTUM DE GLANDE LEGENDA.
• Based on the Twelve Tables; modern example: emergency right of way.

cards.front: EMPHYTEUSIS vs SUPERFICIES — what are they and how are they protected?
cards.back:
Both alienable, hereditary rights in rem against rent: EMPHYTEUSIS to use land, SUPERFICIES to build on it.
• Emphyteuta: almost an owner, pays yearly rent; interdicts and REI VINDICATIO UTILIS.
• Superficiary: INTERDICTUM DE SUPERFICIEBUS; sometimes ACTIO IN FACTUM (DE SUPERFICIE).

cards.front: Exegesis: a Digest fragment is about servitudes — which questions should your interpretation address?
cards.back:
Which servitude exists, what it allows, and how its holder or the owner sues.
• Type: praedial (rural/urban) or personal (USUSFRUCTUS, USUS)?
• Limits: IN FACIENDO NEQUIT, UTILITAS, CIVILITER EXERCENDA, no extension; substance preserved.
• Remedies: VINDICATIO SERVITUTIS vs ACTIO NEGATORIA; extinction by NON USUS, CONFUSIO, death.

cards.front: What is a right of pledge, and why is it valuable to the creditor?
cards.back:
A limited right in rem: the creditor may satisfy an unpaid debt from the proceeds of the pledged thing.
• Enforced by selling it, typically at public auction.
• In bankruptcy: separated from the estate, no sharing with other creditors.
• Ex 36: unsecured Labrax got 30 of 100.

cards.front: Which types of pledge exist?
cards.back:
By origin: contractual, judicial, statutory; by possession: possessory pledge vs non-possessory pledge (lien).
• Possessory: extra security and publicity; pledgee's natural possession is interdict-protected.
• Lien: the pledger keeps using the thing to earn the repayment.

cards.front: Which other securities did Roman law know besides pledge?
cards.back:
Personal guarantee (FIDEIUSSIO) and transfer of ownership by way of security (FIDUCIA CUM CREDITORE).
• FIDEIUSSIO: guarantor liable with all his assets — an obligation, not a right in rem.
• FIDUCIA: creditor becomes owner, must reconvey on payment (a trust).
• Actions: ACTIO FIDUCIAE DIRECTA (debtor) / CONTRARIA (creditor).

cards.front: What three meanings does PIGNUS have, and how do the right and the contract of pledge arise?
cards.back:
The pawn itself, the right in rem (right of pledge), and the real contract of pledge.
• Right of pledge: arises by CONVENTIO PIGNORIS, no delivery needed.
• Contract of pledge: real contract, arises on delivery to the pledgee.
• Lien: contract arises only once the pledgee obtains possession.

cards.front: What are the requirements of a right of pledge as a right in rem?
cards.back:
A secured monetary claim, the pledger's ownership or power of disposal, and a CONVENTIO PIGNORIS.
• Accessorial: no valid claim, no pledge; it ends with the debt.
• Bonitarian ownership suffices; else NEMO PLUS IURIS; later acquisition → convalescence.
• CONVENTIO PIGNORIS = conveyance; fixes the pledged assets and secured debts.

cards.front: What is the ACTIO PIGNERATICIA IN REM?
cards.back:
The pledgee's action in rem (VINDICATIO PIGNORIS) for the pledged thing against any possessor, pledger included.
• Also called ACTIO SERVIANA, QUASI SERVIANA, HYPOTHECARIA.
• Third party failing to restore pays full value; surplus (SUPERFLUUM) goes to the pledger.
• Possessory pledgee vs pledger's REI VINDICATIO: EXCEPTIO PIGNERATICIA.

cards.front: ACTIO PIGNERATICIA IN PERSONAM DIRECTA vs CONTRARIA — who sues for what?
cards.back:
DIRECTA: pledger reclaims the thing or the surplus; CONTRARIA: pledgee claims damages and expenses.
• DIRECTA: return once the debt ends; after sale, the SUPERFLUUM (HYPEROCHA).
• CONTRARIA: eg a sick cow infects the pledgee's calf (Ex 37).
• CONTRARIA also when the pledger delivered a thing without valid pledge.

cards.front: The pledger alienates the pledged thing WITH the creditor's consent — what happens?
cards.back:
Unreserved consent = waiver: the pledge ends, the buyer gets unburdened ownership.
• Consent reserving the pledge: buyer's ownership stays burdened (NEMO PLUS IURIS).
• Marcianus D 20.6.8.14: allowed to sell for 10, sold for 5 → no waiver.
• The claim against the debtor is unaffected.

cards.front: The pledger alienates the pledged thing WITHOUT the creditor's consent — what happens?
cards.back:
The pledge survives: the creditor can demand the thing from any possessor.
• Knowingly selling a movable = FURTUM; the buyer likely gets mere possession.
• No FURTUM (good faith, or land): buyer presumably owner, burdened with the pledge.
• The pledge ends only on destruction (or SPECIFICATIO).

cards.front: How is a pledge enforced?
cards.back:
On default the creditor sells the thing, usually at public auction, and keeps what covers the debt.
• Tacit PACTUM DE VENDENDO (DISTRAHENDO); prior notice (DENUNTIATIO).
• LEX COMMISSORIA (creditor keeps the thing) fell out of use; banned 320 AD.
• Sale ends all pledges; shortfall stays owed; juniors claim surplus by ACTIO UTILIS.

cards.front: What is RES ALIENA PIGNORI DATA, and when does such a pledge convalesce?
cards.back:
Pledging another's thing without authority gives no valid pledge.
• Pledger later becomes owner → pledge convalesces retroactively (Paulus D 13.7.41, case 1).
• Remedy: ACTIO PIGNERATICIA (IN REM) UTILIS — formula requires ownership at pledging.
• Under the real contract, the pledgee may demand a valid pledge (CONTRARIA).

cards.front: Titius pledges E's thing without authority, dies, and E becomes his heir — does the pledge convalesce (Paulus vs Modestinus)?
cards.back:
Paulus (D 13.7.41): no; Modestinus (D 20.1.22): yes, via ACTIO PIGNERATICIA (IN REM) UTILIS.
• Paulus: owner's autonomy — E never meant to burden his property.
• Modestinus: creditor's protection; the heir may be enriched and inherits the debt.

cards.front: On which grounds does a right of pledge end before enforcement?
cards.back:
The debt ends, waiver, CONFUSIO, or the pledged thing ceases to exist.
• Debt paid, acquitted or set off; until then INDIVISA EST PIGNORIS CAUSA.
• Waiver, incl. consent to alienation; CONFUSIO: the creditor becomes owner.
• Destruction or SPECIFICATIO (wood → ship, D 13.7.18.3); USUCAPIO does not end it.

cards.front: Paulus D 20.1.29.2: a pledged house burns down; Lucius Titius buys the land unaware of the pledge and builds. Does the pledge survive?
cards.back:
Yes — the pledge covered house and land (SUPERFICIES SOLO CEDIT), so it persists in land and new house.
• The creditors bring VINDICATIO PIGNORIS against Lucius Titius.
• He has EXCEPTIO DOLI: retains until reimbursed the value increase from building.

cards.front: What is a blanket lien, and what did Scaevola decide about a pledged shop (TABERNA)?
cards.back:
A lien over the pledger's whole present and future property; an aggregate (UNIVERSITAS RERUM) is pledgeable as one.
• Excluded: household items, clothing, personally close slaves.
• D 20.1.34 pr: goods in the shop at death; sold goods are freed.
• D 20.1.34.2: borrowed coins fall under the blanket lien.

cards.front: What is a PIGNUS TACITUM?
cards.back:
A lien implied in certain contracts without an explicit pledge agreement (D 20.2).
• Residential lease: the tenant's INVECTA ILLATA; agricultural lease: the fruits.
• IUS DISPOSITIVUM, not IUS COGENS — the parties may exclude it.

cards.front: Tacit lien in a residential lease vs an agricultural lease — what differs?
cards.back:
Landlord: lien over INVECTA ILLATA with self-help seizure; agricultural lessor: lien over fruits, via VINDICATIO PIGNORIS.
• INVECTA ILLATA: movables brought in to stay; secures rent and damages.
• The tenant reclaims impounded things by INTERDICTUM DE MIGRANDO.
• Lessee's own movables only if explicitly pledged → INTERDICTUM SALVIANUM.

cards.front: What are statutory liens? Give examples.
cards.back:
Liens arising directly from statute or the law as a whole, often as blanket liens.
• Loan for renovating a building (SENATUS CONSULTUM under Marcus Aurelius).
• Fiscal claims; ward over the guardian's property; wife for return of the DOS.

cards.front: What does PRIOR TEMPORE, POTIOR IURE mean for multiple pledges?
cards.back:
'Earlier in time, stronger in law': rank follows order of creation; the senior is satisfied first and fully.
• Multiple liens allowed since the high classical period, to use surplus value.
• Example 38: proceeds 1.000 → Europa 500, Pluto 400, SUPERFLUUM 100 back to pledger Nike.
• Proceeds 800 → Europa 500, Pluto only 300.

cards.front: Africanus D 20.4.9 pr: A leases a bath from 1 July and pledges slave Eros to the lessor; before 1 July he pledges Eros to lender C. Who ranks first?
cards.back:
The lessor — his pledge dates from the earlier contract, not from the start of the lease.
• D 20.4.9.1: a pledge for a conditional claim ranks by its creation date.
• If the condition fails, the pledge ends (accessoriality).

cards.front: How do pledgees assert their rank in court?
cards.back:
By EXCEPTIO and REPLICATIO REI SIBI ANTE PIGNERATAE ('pledged to me earlier').
• Senior possessor vs junior's VINDICATIO PIGNORIS: EXCEPTIO REI SIBI ANTE PIGNERATAE.
• Same rank: MELIOR EST CAUSA POSSIDENTIS — EXCEPTIO REI SIBI QUOQUE PIGNERATAE.
• Junior possessor pleads QUOQUE; senior replies REPLICATIO REI SIBI ANTE PIGNERATAE.

cards.front: What is the IUS OFFERENDI AC SUCCEDENDI?
cards.back:
A junior pledgee may pay off a senior one and step into his rank.
• The most senior decides when to sell.
• Ex 38: Pluto pays Europa 500 → senior rank for 500, plus his 400.
• Tryphoninus D 20.4.20: S's pledge in the HYPEROCHA beats T's later loan.

cards.front: Which exceptions break the principle of priority?
cards.back:
Privileged statutory liens, loans preserving or improving the thing, and agreed succession on refinancing.
• Statutory privilege: ward's, wife's (DOS) and fiscal liens.
• Repair loan ranks first — it raised the value (Ex 39; Ulpianus D 20.4.5).
• Conversion: the new creditor takes the old rank; juniors are unaffected.

cards.front: Exegesis: a Digest fragment is about pledge — which questions should your interpretation address?
cards.back:
Was a valid pledge created, does it still exist, and who enforces it against whom?
• Creation: secured claim (accessoriality), pledger's ownership/disposal, CONVENTIO PIGNORIS and its scope.
• Survival: alienation with/without consent, destruction, SPECIFICATIO, convalescence.
• Remedies and rank: VINDICATIO PIGNORIS, EXCEPTIO DOLI, PRIOR TEMPORE, IUS OFFERENDI.

cards.front: What is an exegesis, and what does it train?
cards.back:
Explaining a Roman source text — usually a classical jurist's decision in the Digest — and giving reasons for it.
• Trains interpreting a text and justifying a pre-existing decision.
• Shows your knowledge of Roman law.
• Unlike case solving, the decision is already given.

cards.front: What is the outline of an exam exegesis?
cards.back:
Four parts: facts of the case, legal question, the jurist's decision, interpretation.
• Keep the first three brief; infer facts the jurist tacitly assumes.
• The interpretation is the main part.
• Scholarly version adds text, translation and INSCRIPTIO.

cards.front: What should go into the interpretation of an exegesis?
cards.back:
A dogmatic classification of the decision and the values behind it.
• Institution and terms; who wants what from whom, on which legal basis.
• Remedy, claimant/defendant, EXCEPTIONES, REPLICATIONES.
• Related cases, juristic controversies, the parties' interests.

cards.front: What does the INSCRIPTIO 'D 20.1.29.2 PAULUS LIBRO QUINTO RESPONSORUM' tell you?
cards.back:
Digest book 20, title 1, fragment 29, paragraph 2 — from book 5 of Paulus' RESPONSA.
• Paulus: a late classical jurist.
• A RESPONSUM already gives facts, question and decision.

cards.front: Model exegesis of D 20.1.29.2: what is the point of Paulus' decision?
cards.back:
The pledge survives the fire and covers the new building, but the bona fide builder is reimbursed.
• House pledge includes the land (SUPERFICIES SOLO CEDIT); sale without consent is no waiver.
• VINDICATIO PIGNORIS vs EXCEPTIO DOLI (retention); MALAE FIDEI builder: only IUS TOLLENDI.
• Balances the creditor's security against the builder's added value.
